steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released a demo of ChatGPT, which is a chatbot powered by a large language model (LLM). The chatbot was impressively able to have conversations and give information, and it got international attention right away, with over one million users in only a few days. LLMs had been actively developed for several years, and they build on technologies that have been researched and used for decades, but the release of ChatGPT was still heralded as a disruptive moment. In that moment the general population, and also many technologists, became aware that AI's capabilities had made a significant leap.

After that, generative AI systems such as ChatGPT, Bard, DALL \cdot E, Imagen, and Midjourney were taken up rapidly, and this came with striking narratives. These narratives talk about its increased ability to do complex tasks and predict how generative AI will disrupt knowledge industries. Knowledge industries are industries like law, journalism, software development, and more, where workers use knowledge they gained through specialized training to do non-routine problem solving and develop products and services. In these narratives generative AI is imagined as a resource that can automate a lot of the knowledge work that humans do now, and so it would have detrimental effects on labor, like eliminating significant numbers of jobs across multiple industries. However, even though initial evidence points to productivity gains when generative AI is used for particular tasks, a lot is still unknown about its future impact.

- Our study
  - unique, timely moment to consider expectations of future use
  - three-hour participatory research workshops, seven knowledge industries, 54 participants, three US cities
- Contributions
  - novel qualitative study, seven fields: advertising, business communications, education, journalism, law, mental health, software development; beyond task/job automation -> shifts in nature and structure of work
  - dominant narrative across industries: generative AI as tool for menial work under human review; unique perspectives per industry
  - social forces in parallel to generative AI frame expectations: deskilling, dehumanization, disconnection, disinformation
  - five HCI research challenges at intersection of generative AI and knowledge work
- Roadmap
  - background, methodology, findings, implications and research challenges for HCI, conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released a demo of ChatGPT, which is a chatbot powered by a large language model (LLM). The chatbot was impressively able to have conversations and give information, and it got international attention right away, with over one million users in only a few days. LLMs had been actively developed for several years, and they build on technologies that have been researched and used for decades, but the release of ChatGPT was still heralded as a disruptive moment. In that moment the general population, and also many technologists, became aware that AI's capabilities had made a significant leap.

After that, generative AI systems such as ChatGPT, Bard, DALL \cdot E, Imagen, and Midjourney were taken up rapidly, and this came with striking narratives. These narratives talk about its increased ability to do complex tasks and predict how generative AI will disrupt knowledge industries. Knowledge industries are industries like law, journalism, software development, and more, where workers use knowledge they gained through specialized training to do non-routine problem solving and develop products and services. In these narratives generative AI is imagined as a resource that can automate a lot of the knowledge work that humans do now, and so it would have detrimental effects on labor, like eliminating significant numbers of jobs across multiple industries. However, even though initial evidence points to productivity gains when generative AI is used for particular tasks, a lot is still unknown about its future impact.

This is a unique moment in the uptake of generative AI and it is a timely opportunity to think deeply about what people expect of its future use. We wanted to understand better how people anticipate generative AI may affect knowledge work in the future, so we conducted three-hour participatory research workshops for seven different knowledge industries. In total there were 54 participants across three US cities. Our contributions are:

- We present a new qualitative study of how knowledge workers in seven professional fields (advertising, business communications, education, journalism, law, mental health, and software development) expect generative AI may affect their fields in the future. We look at knowledge workers' perceptions not only of how specific tasks or jobs might be automated or change in other ways, but also how and whether generative AI might shift the nature and structure of work in their industries more broadly.

- We describe a dominant narrative about generative AI that participants envisioned across multiple knowledge industries, where generative AI is a tool that does menial work under human review. We also highlight perspectives that are unique to each industry.

- We describe specific social forces that participants are experiencing in their industries in parallel to the development of generative AI. These forces include deskilling, dehumanization, disconnection, and disinformation. Together they create a unique confluence of circumstances that frames participants' expectations of generative AI's impact, as it intersects with social trends around its deployment and use.

- Based on our participants' insights, we identify five HCI research challenges where generative AI and knowledge work intersect.

In the rest of the paper we review relevant background, describe our methodology, and present our findings. Then we discuss implications and research challenges for the HCI community, and we conclude.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released a demo of ChatGPT, a chatbot powered by a large language model (LLM). The chatbot's impressive ability to converse and provide information immediately drew international attention, attracting over one million users in just a few days [1]. While LLMs had been under active development for several years, and build on technologies that have been researched and used for decades, ChatGPT's release was heralded as a disruptive moment in which the general population, as well as many technologists, became aware of a significant leap in AI's capabilities.

Since then, the rapid uptake of generative AI systems such as ChatGPT [2], Bard [3], DALL \cdot E [4], Imagen [5], and Midjourney [6] has been accompanied by striking narratives. These include discussion of its increased ability to perform complex tasks and predictions about how generative AI will disrupt knowledge industries (industries such as law, journalism, software development, and more, in which workers apply knowledge gained through specialized training to non-routine problem solving and develop products and services [7]). These narratives imagine generative AI as a resource that can automate much of the knowledge work currently done by humans, with detrimental effects on labor such as eliminating significant numbers of jobs across multiple industries [8]. However, while initial evidence points to productivity gains when generative AI is used for particular tasks [9,10], much remains unknown about its future impact.

This unique moment in the uptake of generative AI offers a timely opportunity to consider expectations of its future use in depth. To better understand how people anticipate generative AI may affect knowledge work in the future, we conducted three-hour participatory research workshops for seven different knowledge industries, with a total of 54 participants across three US cities. Our contributions are as follows:

- • We present a novel qualitative study of how knowledge workers in seven professional fields—advertising, business communications, education, journalism, law, mental health, and software development—expect generative AI may affect their fields in the future. In particular, we explore knowledge workers' perceptions not only of how specific tasks or jobs might be automated or otherwise change, but also of how and whether generative AI might more broadly shift the nature and structure of work in their industries.

- • We describe a dominant narrative about generative AI that participants across multiple knowledge industries envisioned, of generative AI as a tool to perform menial work under human review, and we also highlight unique perspectives from each industry.

- • We describe how specific social forces that participants are experiencing in their industries—in parallel to the development of generative AI—create a unique confluence of circumstances that frames participants' expectations of generative AI's impact as it intersects with social trends around its deployment and use. These forces include deskilling, dehumanization, disconnection, and disinformation.

- • Building on our participants' insights, we identify five HCI research challenges at the intersection of generative AI and knowledge work.

In the rest of the paper, we review relevant background, describe our methodology, present our findings, discuss implications and research challenges for the HCI community, and conclude.
